sets.t: Update on (Approach to) Anemia: Essay questions
Update on (Approach to) Anemia: Essay questions

faq.a: Ferritin rises with inflammation, masking iron deficiency; use transferrin saturation or clinical response to iron.
faq.q: Why is ferritin unreliable in infection?

faq.a: Yes, chronic low‑grade parasitemia can cause hemolysis and marrow suppression, presenting mainly as fatigue.
faq.q: Can malaria cause anemia without fever?

faq.a: When Hb <7 g/dL or <8 g/dL with symptoms, cardiac disease, pregnancy, or active bleeding.
faq.q: When is a blood transfusion indicated?

exam: A 28‑year‑old woman with menorrhagia presents with Hb 9 g/dL – what is your next diagnostic step and why? — Check CBC indices and ferritin to differentiate iron deficiency from chronic disease.
A patient with known sickle cell disease has Hb 6 g/dL and chest pain — what immediate management is required? — Give oxygen, analgesia, consider transfusion, and rule out acute chest syndrome.
In a malaria‑endemic area, a child has pallor and Hb 8 g/dL but normal ferritin — how do you interpret this? — Ferritin may be elevated by infection; assess retic count and treat malaria first.

You have only a CBC and smear available; how would you narrow the cause of a macrocytic anemia? — Look for hypersegmented neutrophils (B12/folate) and consider dietary history; if unavailable, give empirical folate.
A pregnant woman at 20 weeks has Hb 10 g/dL; what are the key investigations and management? — Repeat CBC, assess ferritin, give oral iron, counsel on diet, and monitor fetal growth.

A patient with HIV on antiretroviral therapy presents with Hb 7 g/dL — what causes should you consider and how would you investigate? — Consider zidovudine‑induced marrow suppression, opportunistic infections, and chronic disease; obtain CBC, retic, iron studies, and screen for TB.
When is a bone marrow biopsy indicated in anemia in a low‑resource setting? — When peripheral smear is non‑diagnostic, retic count is low, and common causes have been excluded.
Why is oral iron given with vitamin C and not with tea? — Vitamin C enhances iron absorption; tannins in tea inhibit it.
ai.title: Approach to Anemia
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: A step‑by‑step framework for evaluating anemia in low‑resource settings, focusing on bedside assessment, pragmatic investigations and management of common tropical causes.

b: Hb <13 g/dL in men, <12 g/dL in non‑pregnant women, <11 g/dL in pregnant women.
Confirm with a complete blood count (CBC) and peripheral smear.
sections.p: Anemia is a reduction in hemoglobin (Hb) concentration below age‑ and sex‑specific normal ranges, leading to inadequate oxygen delivery.

b: Mild: Hb 10–12 g/dL (women) or 11–13 g/dL (men).
Moderate: Hb 8–9.9 g/dL.
Severe: Hb <8 g/dL; consider transfusion if symptomatic or unstable.
sections.p: Severity guides urgency of treatment and need for transfusion.

b: Decreased production – iron deficiency (diet, chronic blood loss, hookworm), folate/B12 deficiency, chronic disease (TB, HIV, CKD), marrow suppression (malaria, schistosomiasis).
Increased loss – overt GI bleeding, menorrhagia, parasitic infestations, postpartum hemorrhage.
Increased destruction – sickle cell disease, hereditary spherocytosis, malaria, hemolytic transfusion reactions.
sections.p: Classify by the underlying defect: decreased production, increased loss, or increased destruction.

b: Fatigue, dyspnea on exertion, palpitations, dizziness.
Pallor of conjunctivae, nail beds, palms; tachycardia; systolic flow murmur.
Severe anemia: chest pain, hypotension, altered mental status.
sections.p: Symptoms reflect tissue hypoxia; signs depend on chronicity and severity.
Select tests that answer specific clinical questions; adapt when resources are limited.

t.b: Is anemia microcytic, normocytic or macrocytic? Guides differential (iron vs. B12/folate vs. chronic disease).
What morphological clues are present? (e.g., hypochromic microcytes, sickle cells, schistocytes).
Is iron deficiency present? Low ferritin confirms deficiency; if unavailable, use transferrin saturation or RBC indices.
Is bone marrow responding? Low retic suggests production problem; high retic suggests hemolysis or loss.
Is there chronic GI blood loss? Positive test prompts endoscopic evaluation.

t.a: HIV test, TB screening (GeneXpert or sputum microscopy)
t.b: Are chronic infections contributing? Positive results direct disease‑specific therapy.
Is a macrocytic deficiency present? Low levels confirm need for replacement.

b: Hb <7 g/dL with cardiac disease or pregnancy.
Acute drop in Hb >2 g/dL within 24 h.
Signs of heart failure, chest pain, syncope.
Severe hemolysis with jaundice, dark urine, renal impairment.
sections.p: Identify patients who need urgent intervention.

b: Chronic disease – treat TB, HIV, malaria, or CKD; consider erythropoietin if available and iron replete.
Sickle cell crisis – analgesia, hydration, treat infection, consider transfusion if severe.
Severe anemia – transfuse packed RBCs if Hb <7 g/dL or symptomatic; monitor for transfusion reactions.
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first, then provide supportive care.

b: Re‑check Hb in 2–4 weeks after starting therapy.
Educate on dietary iron (meat, legumes, dark leafy greens) and deworming.
Screen pregnant women early for anemia.
Vaccinate against malaria and provide insecticide‑treated nets.
sections.p: Ensure resolution of cause and monitor response.

b: Hypothyroidism – can cause fatigue and pallor but normal Hb; check TSH.
Chronic heart failure – dyspnea and fatigue but primary problem is cardiac output.
Acute infection – may cause anemia of inflammation; differentiate by retic count and iron studies.
sections.p: Conditions that mimic anemia or share similar signs.

b: Ferritin is an acute‑phase reactant; may be normal/high in inflammation despite iron deficiency.
Peripheral smear may miss early sickle cells; consider sickling test if suspicion high.
Reticulocyte count can be falsely low if sample is delayed; process promptly.
sections.p: Pitfalls in interpretation, especially in low‑resource labs.

whenToSeekHelp: Signs of heart failure (pulmonary edema, peripheral edema)
Rapid Hb fall >2 g/dL in 24 h
